presets.title: Voltage divider
presets.summary: Two resistors split a voltage. Change the values and watch the output and currents.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what will V(out) be?
predict.explain: The same current flows through both resistors, so each drops a share of the supply in proportion to its resistance: V_out = V_in·R2/(R1+R2) = 12·4.7k/14.7k ≈ 3.84 V.

lab.label: R2 is now 10 kΩ, equal to R1 (supply still 12 V). What will V(out) be?
lab.explain: Equal resistors share the voltage equally: V_out = V_in·R2/(R1+R2) = 12·½ = 6 V.

lab.label: Now double the input to 24 V (R1 and R2 both still 10 kΩ). What will V(out) be?
lab.explain: The ratio is fixed by the resistors, so the output scales with the input: 24·½ = 12 V.

lab.label: Replace both resistors with 1 kΩ (input still 24 V). What will V(out) be now?
lab.explain: Only the ratio matters for the unloaded output; scaling both resistors by 1/10 changes the current (12 mA) but not V_out.

presets.title: Two-source network
presets.summary: Two supplies feed a resistor network. Write G·v = i for nodes a and b, predict both voltages, then run .op.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what will V(a) be?
predict.explain: G = [[2, −0.5], [−0.5, 2]] mS (1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 on a's diagonal, −1/R2 between a and b) and i = (12 V/1 kΩ, 5 V/2 kΩ) = (12, 2.5) mA. Determinant 3.75 mS², so V_a = (12 × 2 + 0.5 × 2.5)/3.75 = 6.73 V.

lab.label: V2 is raised to 10 V; nothing else changes. What will V(a) be now?
lab.explain: Only i_b changes, to 10 V/2 kΩ = 5 mA: G is the resistors and hasn't changed. V_a = (12 × 2 + 0.5 × 5)/3.75 = 7.07 V.

lab.label: R2 is now 1 MΩ (V2 still 10 V). What will V(a) be?
lab.explain: G_ab is now only −1 µS: a and b barely interact. a is almost the R1–R3 divider, 12 V × 2 kΩ/3 kΩ = 8 V (7.997 V exactly).

lab.label: R2 is back to 2 kΩ and R3 drops to 1 kΩ (V2 still 10 V). What will V(b) be?
lab.explain: G_aa = 1 + 0.5 + 1 = 2.5 mS, G_bb = 2 mS, G_ab = −0.5 mS; i = (12, 5) mA. Determinant 4.75 mS²: V_b = (2.5 × 5 + 0.5 × 12)/4.75 = 3.89 V. A change at a moves b too, through R2.

lab.label: Superposition: V2 is set to 0 V and R3 is back to 2 kΩ, the original circuit with V2 zeroed. What will V(a) be? This is V1's share.
lab.explain: V2 at 0 V is a wire, so R5 runs from b to ground beside R4: 1 kΩ ∥ 2 kΩ = 0.667 kΩ. Add R2: 2.667 kΩ, in parallel with R3: 1.143 kΩ. V_a = 12 V × 1.143/(1 + 1.143) = 6.40 V. In G·v = i only i changes, to (12, 0) mA: V_a = 12 × 2/3.75 = 6.40 V.

lab.label: Now V1 is set to 0 V and V2 is back to 5 V. What will V(a) be? This is V2's share.
lab.explain: V1 at 0 V is a wire, so R1 sits in parallel with R3: 0.667 kΩ. In G·v = i, i = (0, 2.5) mA: V_a = 0.5 × 2.5/3.75 = 0.333 V. The two shares, 6.40 V + 0.333 V, add to the 6.73 V of the first prediction, with both supplies on.

presets.title: Wheatstone bridge with a meter
presets.summary: A bridge with a meter between its midpoints: predict the meter current from R·i = v, then balance the bridge.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what current will the meter carry, from c to d?
predict.explain: Three clockwise meshes: R = [[3.2k, −1k, −2.2k], [−1k, 3.67k, −470], [−2.2k, −470, 3.67k]] Ω, v = (5, 0, 0) V. The meter carries I_3 − I_2 = 5 V × (2.2k × 2.2k − 1k × 1k)/det = 1.02 mA.

lab.label: R4 is now 4.84 kΩ, so R1·R4 = R2·R3. What will V(d) be?
lab.explain: Balanced: R4/R3 = R2/R1, so d sits where c does, 5 V × 2.2k/3.2k = 3.44 V, and the meter carries no current.

lab.label: Still balanced, the meter is swapped for one of 10 kΩ. What will V(c) be?
lab.explain: At balance the meter carries no current, so its resistance changes nothing: still 3.44 V. That is why a bridge measures by a null.

lab.label: R4 goes back to 1 kΩ, with the 10 kΩ meter. What current will the meter carry, from c to d?
lab.explain: Unbalanced again: R_22 = R_33 = 13.2 kΩ now, and the mesh solve gives 5 V × 3.84 kΩ²/116.48 kΩ³ = 0.165 mA, far less than the 470 Ω meter's 1.02 mA. A higher-resistance meter loads the bridge less, and reads less current.

presets.title: Voltage amplifier model
presets.summary: A sensor (v_s behind R_s) drives an amplifier model, R_in, a dependent source A_vo·v_in and R_out, into a load R_L. Predict the loaded output from the two dividers, then run .op.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what will V(out) be?
predict.explain: Input divider: v_in = 20 mV × 100 kΩ/110 kΩ = 18.18 mV. The dependent source gives A_vo·v_in = 50 × 18.18 mV = 909.1 mV. Output divider: v_o = 909.1 mV × 2.2 kΩ/2.4 kΩ = 833.3 mV. The loaded gain is 41.7, not 50.

schematic.noBuild: an amplifier model: R_in, A_vo·v_in and R_out stand for the amplifier

lab.label: A second, identical load goes in parallel: R_L is now 1.1 kΩ. What will V(out) be?
lab.explain: The input side doesn't see the load: A_vo·v_in is still 909.1 mV. The output divider is now 1.1 kΩ/(200 Ω + 1.1 kΩ) = 0.846, so v_o = 769.2 mV.

lab.label: The sensor is swapped for one with R_s = 100 kΩ (R_L still 1.1 kΩ). What will V(out) be?
lab.explain: R_s now equals R_in, so only half of v_s reaches the input: v_in = 10 mV, A_vo·v_in = 500 mV, and v_o = 500 mV × 0.846 = 423.1 mV.

lab.label: The amplifier is swapped for one with R_in = 1 MΩ, the same A_vo and R_out. What will V(out) be?
lab.explain: R_in is ten times R_s again: v_in = 20 mV × 1 MΩ/1.1 MΩ = 18.18 mV, A_vo·v_in = 909.1 mV, v_o = 769.2 mV. What matters is the ratio of R_in to R_s, not either value alone.

lab.label: A buffered output brings R_out down to 20 Ω. What will V(out) be now?
lab.explain: The output divider is 1.1 kΩ/1.12 kΩ = 0.982, so v_o = 909.1 mV × 0.982 = 892.9 mV, within 2% of A_vo·v_in.

presets.title: RC low-pass filter
presets.summary: Step response (charging with τ = RC) and frequency response (−3 dB at 1/(2πRC)) of the same circuit.

predict.label: Before you simulate: at what frequency is the output 3 dB down?
predict.explain: At f_c the capacitor's reactance 1/(2πfC) equals R, and the output is 1/√2 of the input (−3 dB): f_c = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π·1k·100n) ≈ 1.59 kHz.

lab.label: R is now 2.2 kΩ (C still 100 nF). What is the new cutoff frequency?
lab.explain: f_c = 1/(2πRC) is inversely proportional to R: 2.2× the resistance gives 1/2.2 the cutoff, 723 Hz.

lab.label: Keep R = 2.2 kΩ and shrink C to 10 nF. What is the cutoff now?
lab.explain: C fell tenfold, so f_c rose tenfold: 7.23 kHz.

presets.title: Half-wave rectifier with a reservoir capacitor
presets.summary: A diode charges the capacitor on each positive peak; the load discharges it in between, leaving ripple.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what is the peak output voltage?
predict.explain: The capacitor charges to the input peak less the diode's forward drop while it conducts: 10 V − about 0.7 V ≈ 9.3 V.

lab.label: First, the ripple as it is (100 µF, 1 kΩ, 60 Hz, about 9.3 V peak). Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple with ΔV ≈ I/(fC); expect it to come out roughly 20% high, because the capacitor recharges before a full period has passed and the load current falls as the voltage droops.
lab.explain: I ≈ 9.3 V/1 kΩ = 9.3 mA, so I/(fC) = 9.3 mA/(60 Hz·100 µF) ≈ 1.55 V. The simulated ripple is about 1.3 V: the capacitor starts recharging before the full period is over, and the load current falls as the voltage droops.

lab.label: Raise C to 470 µF. What is the ripple now?
lab.explain: Ripple ≈ I/(fC): 4.7× the capacitance gives about 1/4.7 the ripple.

lab.label: Keep 470 µF but load it harder: R_L = 220 Ω. What is the ripple?
lab.explain: 4.5× the load current gives about 4.5× the ripple.

presets.title: Common-emitter amplifier
presets.summary: Divider bias, a bypassed emitter resistor, and coupling capacitors: a small sine in, a larger inverted sine out.

lab.label: Raise R_E to 2.2 kΩ. The base sits near 2.1 V. What DC voltage will the emitter settle at (average V(e))?
lab.explain: V_E = V_B − V_BE ≈ 2.1 − 0.65 ≈ 1.4 V, almost the same as with R_E = 1 kΩ (1.37 V). R_E sets the current, not the emitter voltage.

lab.label: Still R_E = 2.2 kΩ: with I_C ≈ V_E/R_E, what is the average collector voltage, V(c)?
lab.explain: I_C ≈ V_E/R_E = 1.43 V/2.2 kΩ ≈ 0.65 mA, so R_C drops about 3.0 V and V_C ≈ 12 − 3.0 = 9.0 V.

presets.title: Inverting amplifier with a real op amp
presets.summary: Gain −Rf/Rin until the op amp runs out of gain-bandwidth, slew rate, or supply voltage.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what is the peak output voltage?
predict.explain: The gain is −R_f/R_in = −10, so the 0.5 V peak input gives 5 V peak (inverted). At 1 kHz the op amp has gain-bandwidth to spare, and the output's fastest slope, 2π·1 kHz·5 V ≈ 31 kV/s, is far below the 500 kV/s slew rate.

lab.label: Raise Rf to 47 kΩ (gain −47) with the 0.5 V input. The op amp runs from ±15 V, and like most op amps its output saturates about 1.5 V inside each rail. What peak output will you see?
lab.explain: The ideal output, 47·0.5 = 23.5 V peak, would need more than the supply. The output saturates 1.5 V inside each rail, so the sine is clipped flat at about +13.5 V and −13.5 V.

lab.label: Rf = 100 kΩ (gain −100) and a 50 mV input. With GBW = 1 MHz, what is the −3 dB bandwidth?
lab.explain: Bandwidth ≈ GBW/noise gain = 1 MHz/(1 + 100k/1k) ≈ 9.9 kHz.

presets.title: MOSFET switch with inductive load
presets.summary: A low-side MOSFET chops current through a coil; when the switch opens, the flyback diode D1 (through the clamp resistor RS) carries the coil current. C_oss is the MOSFET's own drain-to-source capacitance, and DB its body diode.

lab.label: With D1 clamping the coil (RS = 0.1 Ω), how high does the drain voltage go when the MOSFET turns off?
lab.explain: The coil's current (about 0.7 A by the end of each on-time, once the cycles settle) cannot stop instantly: v = L·di/dt. When the MOSFET opens, the drain rises until D1 conducts and the current has a path again, through RL, D1, and RS back to the top of the coil. That holds the drain at V_DD + V_D + I·RS = 12 + 0.79 + 0.07 ≈ 12.9 V. The circulating current then decays with τ = L/(RL + RS) ≈ 1 ms, so about 0.4 A is still flowing when the MOSFET turns on again.

lab.label: Set RS to 1 MΩ: D1's path is now practically open, as if the diode were removed, and only the MOSFET's 220 pF C_oss can take the coil current. How high does the drain go now?
lab.explain: With nowhere else to go, the current charges C_oss. Each on-time now starts from zero (there is no clamp loop for the current to circulate in, and the swing back below ground is caught by the MOSFET's body diode), so the current reaches (12 V/10 Ω)(1 − e^(−0.5 ms/1 ms)) = 0.47 A, storing ½LI² = ½ × 10 mH × (0.47 A)² ≈ 1.1 mJ. That energy moves into the capacitor: ½C·V² = ½L·I², so the drain swings I·√(L/C) = 0.47 A × √(10 mH/220 pF) ≈ 0.47 A × 6.7 kΩ ≈ 3.2 kV above the 12 V supply. A real MOSFET never gets there: it breaks down (avalanches) at or a little above its V_DS rating and must absorb at least that 1.1 mJ itself on every cycle (more, because the supply keeps feeding the coil during the avalanche), over 1 W at 1 kHz. Unless the part is rated for that repetitive avalanche energy, it overheats and fails. The flyback diode gives that energy a safe path.

lab.label: Now RS = 100 Ω: the diode conducts again, but through 100 Ω. How high does the drain go?
lab.explain: At turn-off the coil's 0.47 A has to flow through RS, so the drain rises to V_DD + V_D + I·RS = 12 + 0.77 + 47 ≈ 60 V. In exchange, the current decays with τ = L/(RL + RS) = 10 mH/110 Ω ≈ 91 µs instead of about 1 ms, so it reaches zero well within the 0.5 ms off-time. This is a real design trade-off: a resistor or Zener diode in series with the flyback diode makes a relay release faster, but the MOSFET must be rated for the higher spike.

lab.label: Back to RS = 0.1 Ω, with a coil ten times larger: L = 100 mH. How high does the drain go now?
lab.explain: Still about V_DD + V_D ≈ 12.8 V. With a clamp, the diode sets the spike's height, not the coil. The coil sets the timing: τ = L/RL = 100 mH/10 Ω = 10 ms, ten times longer. The current climbs only about 50–60 mA per on-time (di/dt ≈ 12 V/100 mH = 120 A/s at first, less as I·RL grows), loses only about 7–14 mA per off-time, and is still building up (0.23 A) when this 5 ms run ends. A larger coil holds its energy ½LI² for longer, and through a plain diode that energy takes several L/R to die away. That is why a big relay clamped by a diode alone releases slowly.

presets.title: Zener regulator
presets.summary: Sweep the input: while the divider output V_in·R_L/(R_S+R_L) is below V_Z the Zener is off and the output follows it; once it would exceed V_Z, the Zener conducts and the output flattens at about V_Z.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what will V(out) be at the top of the sweep?
predict.explain: Without the Zener the divider would give 15·1k/1.22k ≈ 12.3 V, far above V_Z, so the Zener conducts and takes whatever current holds the output near 5.1 V. R_S drops the rest, about 9.9 V.

lab.label: A much heavier load: RL = 100 Ω. What will V(out) be at the top of the 15 V sweep?
lab.explain: With R_L = 100 Ω the divider alone gives 15·100/320 = 4.69 V, below V_Z, so the Zener never conducts.

lab.label: Keep RL = 100 Ω and lower the series resistor to 100 Ω. What is V(out) at 15 V now? (R_S now dissipates about 1 W: size it accordingly.)
lab.explain: The divider alone would now give 15·100/200 = 7.5 V, above V_Z, so the Zener conducts and clamps the output near 5.1 V (5.16 V). R_S carries (15 − 5.16)/100 ≈ 98 mA: 52 mA to the load, the rest through the Zener.

presets.title: Schmitt trigger vs plain comparator
presets.summary: The same sine, with a 50× faster interfering tone added, drives a plain comparator (it chatters at each crossing) and a Schmitt trigger (it switches once).

lab.label: First the plain comparator. The 1 V sine now carries a 0.1 V interfering tone at 50 times its frequency. A clean sine would make it switch twice per period, once at each zero crossing. With the interference, how many times does it switch per period? (An estimate is enough: within 50% counts.)
lab.explain: A comparator without hysteresis switches every time its input crosses 0 V. Near each zero crossing the sine changes slowly (slope 2πf·1 V), while the tone's slope reaches 2π·50f·0.1 V, five times steeper. So the tone drags the sum back and forth across zero for as long as the sine is within 0.1 V of zero: about ±0.1 rad, 1.6 cycles of the tone. The sum ends on the opposite side from where it started, so each clean crossing becomes an odd number of crossings. Here both sources start at phase 0, and solving sin x + 0.1·sin 50x = 0 gives 5 crossings around the rising zero crossing and 3 around the falling one: 8 switches per period instead of 2. The exact count depends on the tone's phase at each crossing; the mechanism does not.

lab.label: Now the Schmitt trigger. The op amps run from ±5 V, so V_sat = 5 V and the Schmitt thresholds are ±V_sat·R1/R2 = ±0.5 V. How many times does its output switch during one period of the signal?
lab.explain: Once the output switches, the threshold moves to the other side of zero by 0.5 V. The ±0.1 V interference cannot bring the input back across it.

lab.label: Lower R2 to 20 kΩ. How many times does the Schmitt output switch per period now?
lab.explain: The thresholds are now ±5·10k/20k = ±2.5 V. The input peaks at only about 1.1 V, so it never reaches either threshold and the output never changes state.

lab.label: Back to R2 = 100 kΩ (±0.5 V), with three times the interference (0.3 V). How many switches per period?
lab.explain: The interference is 0.6 V peak to peak, still less than the 1 V gap between the thresholds.

presets.title: H-bridge motor driver
presets.summary: Two half-bridges drive a motor (modeled as L and R). Swapping which diagonal is on reverses the current. Real drivers add a short dead time between turning one transistor off and its partner on; without it both conduct for an instant and short the supply (shoot-through).

lab.label: Halve the motor's winding resistance to 2 Ω (still 1 mH, 12 V, 200 Hz). What peak current flows now? (Each MOSFET is about 0.02 Ω when on.)
lab.explain: Steady current = V/(R_m + 2R_on) = 12/2.04 ≈ 5.9 A. With τ = L/R ≈ 0.5 ms and 2.5 ms per direction, the current gets within about 1% of it (5.8 A).

lab.label: Back to 4 Ω, but reverse ten times faster: 2 kHz. With L/R = 0.25 ms, does the current still reach 3 A? What peak do you expect? (In steady state the current swings symmetrically between −I_pk and +I_pk.)
lab.explain: Each half-period (0.25 ms) is only about one τ, so the current never settles. In steady state it swings symmetrically between ±I·tanh(t_half/2τ) = ±2.97 A·tanh(0.5) ≈ ±1.4 A.

presets.title: Buck converter
presets.summary: A PMOS switch chops the input, a diode freewheels the inductor current, and the LC filter averages it: V_out ≈ D·V_in.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what average output voltage do you expect?
predict.explain: While the switch is on, sw sits at V_in; while it is off, the freewheeling diode holds sw about 0.5 V below ground. The LC filter passes the average: V_out ≈ D·V_in − (1−D)·V_D = 6 − 0.5·0.5 ≈ 5.75 V.

lab.label: Set the duty cycle to 0.25. Roughly what average output voltage will the buck give? (Its diode drops about 0.5 V while it conducts.)

presets.title: Diode I–V curve
presets.summary: Sweep the voltage across a silicon diode and watch the current. On a linear axis it looks like almost nothing, then a sharp rise; in fact it grows tenfold for every 60 mV (at n = 1) everywhere above about 0.1 V. VM is a 0 V source used as an ammeter, a standard SPICE trick.
presets.netlist:
Diode I-V curve
VD a 0 0
VM a k 0
D1 k 0 DX
.model DX D(IS={Is} N={N})
.dc VD 0 {Vmax} {Vstep}

predict.label: Before you simulate: how much current flows at the top of the sweep? (I_S = 10 fA, n = 1, V_T = 25.85 mV)
predict.explain: I = I_S·(e^(V/nV_T) − 1) = 10 fA·e^(0.7/0.02585) = 10 fA·e^27.1 ≈ 5.7 mA. The exponent, not I_S, does almost all the work.

lab.label: Sweep only to 0.6 V: 0.1 V less than before (I_S = 10 fA, n = 1). How much current flows at the top now?
lab.explain: At n = 1 the current falls tenfold for every 59.5 mV: 0.1 V lower is ÷48.

lab.label: Keep 0.6 V and set the emission coefficient n = 2. What current flows at 0.6 V? (Model experiment: a real diode with n = 2 would also have a far larger I_S.)
lab.explain: n = 2 doubles the voltage per decade, so the exponent halves: I = I_S·e^(0.6/0.0517) ≈ 1.1 nA.

presets.title: MOSFET transfer curve
presets.summary: Sweep V_GS with V_DS held high: no current below the threshold, then I_D = K(V_GS − V_t)² in saturation.
presets.netlist:
MOSFET transfer curve
VGS g 0 0
VDD dd 0 {Vds}
VM dd d 0
M1 d g 0 NM
.model NM NMOS(VTO={Vt} KP={KP})
.dc VGS 0 {Vgmax} {Vstep}

predict.label: Before you simulate: what drain current flows at the top of the sweep?
predict.explain: With V_DS = 10 V the MOSFET is in saturation, so I_D = K(V_GS − V_t)² = 2 mA/V²·(5 − 2)² = 18 mA.

lab.label: Lower the threshold to 1 V (K = 2 mA/V²). What drain current flows at V_GS = 5 V?
Keep V_t = 1 V and double K to 4 mA/V². What drain current flows at V_GS = 5 V?
lab.explain: I_D is proportional to K: 64 mA.

presets.title: Emitter follower
presets.summary: The emitter follows the base about 0.7 V lower, with a gain just under 1. Its input draws only I_E/(β+1), so a weak source can drive a heavy load.
presets.netlist:
Emitter follower
VCC vcc 0 12
VS in 0 SIN({Vb} {Vs} {f})
Q1 vcc in out QN
RE out 0 {Re}
.model QN NPN(BF=100)
.tran {tstep} {tstop}

predict.label: Before you simulate: what is the average (DC) level of V(out)?
predict.explain: The emitter sits one V_BE below the base. At about 5.3 mA the transistor needs V_BE ≈ 0.70 V, so the output averages 6 − 0.70 ≈ 5.30 V.

lab.label: A heavier emitter load: R_E = 100 Ω, so ten times the emitter current. V_BE grows by about 60 mV per decade of current. What is the average V(out) now?
lab.explain: Ten times the current raises V_BE by about V_T·ln 10 ≈ 60 mV, to about 0.76 V, so the output average falls from 5.30 V to about 5.24 V.

presets.title: Active low-pass filter
presets.summary: An inverting amplifier with a capacitor across R_f: gain −R_f/R_in at low frequencies, falling 20 dB per decade above f_c = 1/(2π R_f C).

predict.label: Before you simulate: what is the cutoff frequency?
predict.explain: At low frequencies the gain is −R_f/R_in = −10. The capacitor in parallel with R_f takes over the feedback once its reactance falls below R_f: f_c = 1/(2πR_fC) = 1/(2π·10k·10n) ≈ 1.59 kHz.

lab.label: Change C to 22 nF (R_f = 10 kΩ). What is the new cutoff frequency?
lab.explain: f_c = 1/(2πR_fC): 2.2× C gives about 723 Hz.

lab.label: Keep C = 22 nF and lower R_f to 4.7 kΩ. What is the cutoff now? (The gain drops too.)
lab.explain: R_f sets both the gain and the cutoff: 1/(2π·4.7k·22n) ≈ 1.54 kHz, and the gain falls to −4.7.

presets.title: Constant-current LED driver
presets.summary: An op amp drives a MOSFET so the sense resistor always holds V_set: the current through the two LEDs (1 W white power LEDs, about 3.1 V at 100 mA) is V_set/R_s whatever the supply does, until the headroom runs out. VM is a 0 V ammeter. The op amp runs from its own 0–15 V supply.
presets.netlist:
LED driver
VS vs 0 {Vs}
VM vs top 0
D1 top a DL
D2 a d DL
M1 d g s NM
RS s 0 {Rs}
VSET set 0 {Vset}
X1 set s g OA
.model DL D(IS=1e-27 N=2)
.model NM NMOS(VTO=2 KP=2)
.model OA OPAMP(A=1e5 VPOS=15 VNEG=0)
.op

predict.label: Before you simulate: how much current flows through the LEDs?
predict.explain: The op amp raises the gate until V(s) equals V_set, so I = V_set/R_s = 0.5 V/4.99 Ω ≈ 100.2 mA. The LEDs and the MOSFET take whatever voltage that current needs.

lab.label: Raise the supply to 15 V (R_s = 4.99 Ω). What LED current flows now?
lab.explain: The loop holds V(R_s) = V_set, so I = V_set/R_s. The extra supply voltage appears across the MOSFET.

lab.label: Halve R_s to 2.49 Ω (supply 15 V). What LED current flows? (The MOSFET now dissipates about 1.7 W: it needs a heat sink.)
lab.explain: I = V_set/R_s = 0.5/2.49 ≈ 200.8 mA, twice the current.

lab.label: Drop the supply to 6 V. Two LEDs at about 3.1 V each plus V_set don't fit, so the op-amp output rises to its rail, the MOSFET is fully on, and regulation is lost. Each LED's voltage falls about 0.12 V for every tenfold drop in current (3.1 V at 100 mA). Roughly how much current flows?
lab.explain: With the MOSFET fully on, 6 V = 2·V_LED + I·2.49 Ω. At about 12 mA each LED needs 3.1 − 0.12·log10(100/12) ≈ 2.99 V, and the two take 5.97 V, leaving only about 30 mV across R_s: the simulator gives 11.8 mA.

presets.title: RL step: coil current rise
presets.summary: A step through R into an inductor: the current starts at zero, rises at V/L, and settles at V/R with τ = L/R. The run ends at the time t you set, so the last point is the current at t.

predict.label: Before you simulate: what current flows in L1 at the end of the run, 417 µs after the step?
predict.explain: τ = L/R = 100 mH / 240 Ω = 417 µs, so the run ends at one τ: 63.2% of 12 V / 240 Ω = 50 mA, which is 31.6 mA. At the first instant the current is zero and all 12 V is across L1 (node a jumps to 12 V); as the current rises, R takes more of the step.

lab.label: R is now 480 Ω. What current flows at the same 417 µs?
lab.explain: The final current halves to 12 V / 480 Ω = 25 mA, and τ = L/R halves to 208 µs, so 417 µs is now 2τ: 25 mA × (1 − e^(−2)) = 21.6 mA. More resistance: less current, reached sooner. An RC circuit does the opposite.

lab.label: Keep R = 480 Ω and use a 47 mH coil. What current flows at 417 µs?
lab.explain: τ = 47 mH / 480 Ω = 97.9 µs, so 417 µs is 4.26τ and the current is within 1.5% of its final value: 25 mA × (1 − e^(−4.26)) = 24.6 mA. L sets only how fast; the final current is V/R whatever L is.

presets.title: RC square-wave response
presets.summary: A square wave from 0 to V into R and C: each edge is a switch event, C's voltage starts each half where the last one ended, and once settled it swings between two fixed levels centered on V/2.

predict.label: Before you simulate: once the trace has settled, how far does C1's voltage swing, peak to peak?
predict.explain: Each half-period, 10 ms, is exactly one τ = RC = 10 kΩ × 1 µF = 10 ms, so each half closes 63.2% of the gap to the input's new level. Settled, C1 swings between V/(1 + e^(−1)) = 3.66 V and 5 V − 3.66 V = 1.34 V: 2.31 V peak to peak, centered on 2.5 V.

lab.label: Slow the square wave to 10 Hz, 50 ms per half. How far does C1 swing now?
lab.explain: Each half is now 5τ, so C1 gets within 1% of each level before the input reverses: x = e^(−5) = 0.0067, and the swing is 5 V × (1 − x)/(1 + x) = 4.93 V. The trace looks like the square wave with rounded corners.

lab.label: Speed it up to 500 Hz, 1 ms per half. How far does C1 swing now?
lab.explain: Each half is only 0.1τ: C1 barely moves before the input reverses. x = e^(−0.1) = 0.905, and the swing is 5 V × (1 − 0.905)/(1 + 0.905) = 0.250 V, a small triangle around 2.5 V; for T/2 much shorter than τ it approaches V·T/(4τ). The RC is averaging the square wave.

presets.title: Series RLC step
presets.summary: A step through R and L into C: the capacitor's voltage overshoots the step and rings at about f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), with ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) setting how far it overshoots and how fast the ringing dies. R stands for all the loop's resistance, the coil's winding included.

predict.label: Before you simulate: how high does C1's voltage go after the 5 V step?
predict.explain: √(L/C) = √(10 mH / 100 nF) = 316 Ω, so ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) = 23.5 Ω / 316 Ω = 0.074: lightly damped. The first peak overshoots the step by e^(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) = e^(−0.234) = 79%, so C1 reaches 5 V × 1.79 = 8.96 V, at t = π/ω_d = 99.6 µs. It then rings at f_d = f₀√(1 − ζ²) = 5.02 kHz, the envelope shrinking as e^(−αt) with α = R/(2L) = 2350 s⁻¹.

lab.label: R is now 220 Ω. How high does C1's voltage go now?
lab.explain: ζ = 110 Ω / 316 Ω = 0.348, so the overshoot is e^(−π × 0.348/√(1 − 0.121)) = e^(−1.166) = 31%: C1 peaks at 5 V × 1.31 = 6.56 V. The ringing frequency hardly moves (4.72 kHz against 5.02 kHz), but each cycle now loses far more of its energy in R: α = R/(2L) = 11 000 s⁻¹, and the ringing is gone within 8L/R = 0.36 ms.

lab.label: R is now 680 Ω. How high does C1's voltage go now?
lab.explain: Critical damping is at R = 2√(L/C) = 632 Ω. At 680 Ω, ζ = 1.08: overdamped. There is no ringing and no overshoot; C1 creeps up to the 5 V step and stops there, so the peak is 5.00 V. Critical damping is the fastest rise that never overshoots; more R than that only slows the rise.
